```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

This article is for authors who keep a weft project in git. It follows one
small report from its first commit to a release check. After it you will
know what the commit gate refuses and how to answer it, what the ledger
records and how `changes()` reads it, and how `verify()` checks a project
before you hand it on.

The examples need git, Quarto and a project set up with `use_weft()`, so
they are not run when this article is built. Each command was run in a
scratch project, and the output shown is what it printed. Paths have been
shortened.

## Three checks, at three moments

weft checks a project at three moments:

| When | What runs | What it reads |
|---|---|---|
| each commit | the commit gate, `gate()` | the static lints of the changed files, compared with `HEAD` |
| each render | the checks in the document | the values, the spans and the claims as they knit |
| before release | `verify()` | everything: lints, a full render, the ledgers |

The **commit gate** is a `commit-msg` git hook that runs `gate()`.
`use_weft()` installs it, or `use_hooks()` on its own. It compares what the
commit will hold with `HEAD`, and refuses the commit for one of three
reasons:

1. a **construct error** in a changed document, whatever `HEAD` held;
2. a **tier-1 finding that `HEAD` did not hold**, such as a newly typed
   number;
3. weft constructs **removed**, when the commit message does not say so.

The gate runs no R code from the project and renders nothing. It reads git
only, so it takes a fraction of a second.

## A report before weft

The report starts as an ordinary Quarto document, committed to git:

````{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
---
title: "Creek report"
---

## Sites {#sec-sites}

```{r}
#| label: data
turbidity <- c(Upper = 4.2, Middle = 7.9, Lower = 12.6)
n_high <- sum(turbidity > 10)
```

We sampled three sites in 2024. One site read above the trigger of 10 NTU.
````

Then the author sets weft up:

```{r}
weft::use_weft()
#> weft will set up creek-report:
#>   use_setup       .Rprofile (new), _weft.yml (new), report.qmd (edit)
#>   use_quarto      _extensions/weft-check/_extension.yml (new), _extensions/weft-check/weft.lua (new), _extensions/weft-check/weftlib/ (new), _extensions/weft-check/weft-check.lua (new), _extensions/weft-check/weft-output.lua (new), _weft/pre-render.R (new), _weft/post-render.R (new), _quarto.yml (edit)
#>   use_dictionary  dict.yml (new), _weft/dict.schema.json (new)
#>   use_hooks       .git/hooks/commit-msg (new)
#>   use_ci          skipped: origin is not on GitHub
#>   use_agent_docs  AGENTS.md (new), .agents/skills/weft/SKILL.md (new), .agents/skills/weft/references/reports.md (new), .agents/skills/weft/references/syntax.md (new)
#> Wrote: .Rprofile, _weft.yml, report.qmd, ...
```

`vignette("setup", package = "weft")` describes each of these files. The
edit to `report.qmd` adds `engine: knitr` to its front matter.

```sh
git add .Rprofile _weft.yml report.qmd _extensions _weft _quarto.yml \
  dict.yml AGENTS.md .agents
git commit -m "Set up weft"
```

```text
commit-msg: weft passed (1 changed file, 0.3 s)
[main 780cac8] Set up weft
 12 files changed, 1041 insertions(+)
```

The report still holds two typed numbers, "2024" and "10". The gate lets
them through, because it refuses only findings that `HEAD` did not hold.
A project can adopt weft without fixing every old number first.

## A new typed number

The author adds a sentence:

```markdown
The highest reading was 12.6 NTU.
```

```sh
git add report.qmd
git commit -m "Report the highest reading"
```

```text
commit-msg: 1 finding added that HEAD did not hold
  report.qmd
       15  numeral  "12.6" is a number typed in prose (rule 5.2.1).
                    Write it as a value, put it in the dictionary, or mark it [12.6]{.weft-literal why="..."}.

commit-msg: 0.3 s
```

The commit is refused. The hint lists the three fixes. Here the number is
computed from data, so the author computes it. The trigger is a choice, so
it goes in `dict.yml`:

```yaml
trigger:
  value: 10
  type: quantity
  unit: NTU
  definition: "Turbidity above which a site is reported."
```

and the report becomes:

````{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
---
title: "Creek report"
engine: knitr
---

## Sites {#sec-sites}

```{r}
#| label: data
turbidity <- u(c(Upper = 4.2, Middle = 7.9, Lower = 12.6), NTU)
n_high <- sum(turbidity > dict$trigger)
```

We sampled three sites in 2024.
[No site | One site | # sites]{n="n_high"} read above the trigger of `r dict$trigger`{.num}.
The highest reading was `r claim(max(turbidity), . < u(50, NTU))`{.num}.
````

```text
$ git add report.qmd dict.yml
$ git commit -m "Compute the highest reading"
commit-msg: weft passed (1 changed file, 0.3 s)
[main db9c980] Compute the highest reading
```

"2024" is still there and still tolerated. `lints()` lists every finding,
old and new, if you want to see what remains (see
`vignette("lints", package = "weft")`).

## The ledger

Each render of a set-up project writes a **ledger** for each document: a
record of every value and every chosen arm the render printed, with the
sentence it sat in. It lives in `_weft/ledger/`, one folder per source:

```text
_weft/ledger/report.qmd/report.jsonl
_weft/ledger/report.qmd/report.conditions.jsonl
```

Commit it with the source. Then git holds what each version of the report
said, and `changes()` can compare them.

```sh
quarto render report.qmd
git add _weft/ledger
git commit -m "Render the report"
```

The ledger is JSON Lines. The first line records what the render read: the
dictionary entries, the source files and any targets, each with a hash. Each
later line is one entry:

```text
{"weft":"ledger","version":1,"source":"report.qmd","output":"report","dict":{"trigger":"8e71a4f3e615896d"},"files":{"report.qmd":"7f971c44b8bcdfd7"},"targets":{}}
{"file":"report.qmd","section":"sec-sites","kind":"n","expr":"n_high","occ":1,"id":null,"context":"prose","text":"No site","arm":"zero","rel":"=","raw":0,"unit":null,"failed":null,"dict":[],"sentence":"No site read above the trigger of 10 NTU."}
{"file":"report.qmd","section":"sec-sites","kind":"value","expr":"dict$trigger","occ":1,"id":null,"context":"prose","text":"10 NTU","arm":null,"rel":"=","raw":10,"unit":"NTU","failed":null,"dict":["dict$trigger"],"sentence":"No site read above the trigger of 10 NTU."}
```

An entry is keyed by its file, its section anchor and its expression. That
is why the lints ask for a `{#id}` on each heading: the key stays the same
when the heading's words change.

A **table** gets one entry too: a table that an R chunk prints, such as
`knitr::kable()`, gt, flextable or tinytable, and text that a chunk with
`results: asis` prints. The entry holds no cells. It holds a digest of the
table's visible text, with the markup taken out, so a change of style,
class name or element id is not a change, and a change of any number or
word is. It is keyed by the chunk's label, and by its place in the chunk
when a chunk prints two:

```text
{"file":"report.qmd","section":"sec-sites","kind":"table","expr":"tbl-sites","occ":1,"id":"tbl-sites","context":"chunk","text":"5c1d0e2f9a7b3c48","arm":null,"rel":null,"raw":null,"unit":null,"failed":null,"dict":[],"sentence":"Turbidity at each site."}
```

The `sentence` is the table's caption, or the start of its text. A table
printed as plain code output (`print(df)` without `results: asis`), a
figure, and a table that a Python or Julia chunk prints in a knitr document
are not recorded. A document on the Jupyter or Julia engine gets the same
entries from the filter, keyed by the label of the cell (see the languages
article); its digest is of the cell text, and does not compare with an R
document's.
Label the chunks that print tables, so that each keeps its name when a
chunk is added above it.

The **condition log**, `report.conditions.jsonl`, records each warning and
error that a chunk or an inline expression raised during the render, and,
for a document that reads targets, the ones recorded in the targets store.
A new warning then shows in the diff, even when the output looks the same.

## What changed: `changes()`

New data arrive. The Lower reading was 9.6, not 12.6, and the author adds a
nitrate column whose values came from a laboratory as text:

```r
turbidity <- u(c(Upper = 4.2, Middle = 7.9, Lower = 9.6), NTU)
n_high <- sum(turbidity > dict$trigger)
nitrate <- as.numeric(c("0.8", "<0.5", "1.1"))
```

After a render, `changes()` compares the ledgers in the working tree with
those in `HEAD`:

```{r}
weft::changes()
#> weft changes since HEAD (9e34dd7): 1 ledger compared; 2 changed, 0 added, 0 removed; 1 new condition
#>
#> Structural changes
#>   ~ report.qmd#sec-sites  n  n_high  [arm one -> zero, crosses 0]
#>       before: One site read above the trigger of 10 NTU.
#>       after:  No site read above the trigger of 10 NTU.
#>
#> Other changes, ranked
#>   ~ report.qmd#sec-sites  value  claim(max(turbidity), . < u(50, NTU))  [claim word "highest"]
#>       before: The highest reading was 12.6 NTU.
#>       after:  The highest reading was 9.6 NTU.
#>
#> New conditions
#>   ! report.qmd  chunk data  warning: NAs introduced by coercion
```

Read it from the top:

- **Structural changes** come first. An arm changed, a value changed sign,
  crossed 0, 1 or a dictionary value, or moved by an order of magnitude.
  These are the changes most likely to make a sentence elsewhere wrong.
- **Other changes, ranked** follow. A change beside a claim word, such as
  "highest" or "all", ranks above a plain change; then larger relative
  changes rank higher.
- **New conditions** lists warnings and errors the last committed render
  did not raise. Here `as.numeric()` turned "<0.5" into `NA`, which the
  output alone would not show.
- **Not re-rendered**, when present, lists ledgers whose inputs (a
  dictionary entry, a source file, a target) changed after the render.
  Their values are stale.

A different value with the same printed text is not a change. `changes()`
also lists tier-2 lint findings on lines added since the commit.

Tables come last, under **Tables**: a changed table by its label, with its
caption under it, and added and removed tables one line per ledger:

```text
Tables
  ~ table `tbl-sites` changed
      Turbidity at each site.
  report.qmd: 1 table added: tbl-flow
```

`changes()` says that a table changed, not which cells; render the two
versions to compare them. The first render after you upgrade to a weft
that records tables lists every table of an existing ledger as added, once.
Commit that ledger, and the next comparison is quiet.

`changes(since = )` compares with any commit, and `print(x, brief = TRUE)`
prints only the header, the structural changes, the stale ledgers and the
new conditions:

```{r}
print(weft::changes(since = "9e34dd7"), brief = TRUE)
#> weft changes since 9e34dd7 (9e34dd7): 1 ledger compared; 1 changed, 0 added, 1 removed; 1 new condition
#>
#> Structural changes
#>   ~ report.qmd#sec-sites  n  n_high  [arm one -> zero, crosses 0]
#>       before: One site read above the trigger of 10 NTU.
#>       after:  No site read above the trigger of 10 NTU.
#>
#> New conditions
#>   ! report.qmd  chunk data  warning: NAs introduced by coercion
```

`changes()` renders nothing and writes nothing.

## Removing constructs

A computed value, a span or a claim is a check. Deleting one is sometimes
right, but it should never happen by accident. The author drops the
sentence on the highest reading:

```{verbatim, lang = "text"}
$ git commit -m "Drop the sentence on the highest reading"
commit-msg: 2 weft constructs removed, and the message does not say so

  report.qmd, as in HEAD
       17  claim(max(turbidity), . < u(50, NTU))
       17  `r claim(max(turbidity), . < u(50, NTU))`{.num}

  If the removal is intended, add this line at the end of the commit
  message, after a blank line:

      Weft-Removed: 2

  or commit with: git commit --trailer "Weft-Removed: 2"

commit-msg: 1 check gone since HEAD (information: what still checks each; rule 6.3.7)
  report.qmd, as in HEAD
       17  max(turbidity) < u(50, NTU)
           looser: no check of max(turbidity) against a quantity in NTU remains in report.qmd

commit-msg: 0.2 s
```

The value and its claim count as two constructs. The removal is intended,
so the author says so:

```text
$ git commit -m "Drop the sentence on the highest reading" --trailer "Weft-Removed: 2"
commit-msg: note: report.qmd:17 in HEAD, `max(turbidity) < u(50, NTU)`, is gone and nothing that remains covers it (rule 6.3.7)
commit-msg: weft passed (1 changed file, 0.2 s)
[main c2ba829] Drop the sentence on the highest reading
```

The note says that nothing else in the document checks the highest
reading now (see "What still checks a removed check" below). It decides
nothing.

The trailer stays in the history, so a reviewer can find every commit that
removed checks with `git log --grep "Weft-Removed"`. The number must match:
a trailer that says 1 when 2 were removed is refused.

### What still checks a removed check

The gate also says, for each check that a commit removes, whether a check
that remains still covers it. A document guards `turb_max >= trigger` in
nine sentences and `turb_max > trigger` in one, at line 64. Deleting the
sentence at line 64 leaves the document looser than it was, and the gate's
report says so after the constructs removed:

```text
commit-msg: 1 check gone since HEAD (information: what still checks each; rule 6.3.7)
  report.qmd, as in HEAD
       64  turb_max > trigger
           looser: nothing that remains implies it; remaining on turb_max against trigger: `turb_max >= trigger` (9 places)
```

These lines are information. They decide nothing: the commit passes or
fails on the constructs removed and the trailer, exactly as above. Each
check that is gone gets one verdict:

| Verdict | Means |
|---|---|
| covered | the same check remains, or a remaining check implies it: `x > 5` implies `x >= 5`, `x > 3` and `x != 5` |
| looser | no remaining check implies it: checks of the same value against the same thing remain but are weaker, or only a warned check implies it (a warned check fails nothing), or nothing checks that value against that thing any more |
| not judged | a name the check reads is assigned in more than one place in the document, so no other check is taken to cover it |
| not read | the check is not a comparison weft reads (see `checks()` in `vignette("wording", package = "weft")`) |
| the document is gone | the file was deleted or renamed, and its checks with it |

One remaining check must cover the removed one alone: `x >= 5` and
`x != 5` together do not cover `x > 5`. A check that does not always run,
in an arm of a span or in a claim under an R `if` or loop, covers nothing.

A changed bound removes no construct, so it needs no trailer. When it
loosens the document, a passing commit prints a note before its line:

```text
commit-msg: note: report.qmd:44 in HEAD, `n_up >= 10`, is gone and nothing that remains covers it (rule 6.3.7)
```

`gate()` returns the rows in `checks`. The way to keep these lines short
is the advice of the wording article: check a value once, where it is made,
and use its name after.

## Construct errors

A construct error is refused in any changed file, even one that held it
before:

```text
$ git commit -m "Say which way turbidity moved"
commit-msg: 1 construct error
  report.qmd
       17  construct  A formatter on an `if` span is an error (rule 1.5.7): .num.

commit-msg: 0.2 s
```

## Running the gate by hand

`gate()` is the function the hook runs. Call it to judge what is staged
without committing:

```{r}
weft::gate()
#> commit-msg: 1 finding added that HEAD did not hold
#>   report.qmd
#>        17  numeral  "3.4" is a number typed in prose (rule 5.2.1).
#>                     Write it as a value, put it in the dictionary, or mark it [3.4]{.weft-literal why="..."}.
#>
#> commit-msg: 0.3 s
```

It returns, invisibly, a list with `ok` and the findings, so a script can
test `weft::gate()$ok`. `gate(message = )` takes the path of a file holding
a commit message, to check a `Weft-Removed` trailer. It judges the whole
repository, including every subfolder that holds a `_weft.yml`.

## The hook

`use_hooks()` writes `.git/hooks/commit-msg`. The script is POSIX `sh` and
starts:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
# weft-file: use_hooks 0.1.0 063f9359c3c3c3c91daa6def625f32d8
# The weft commit gate (rules 6.1 to 6.3), written by weft::use_hooks().
# Remove it with weft::use_hooks(remove = TRUE). Skip it for one commit
# with: git commit --no-verify
```

It records the `Rscript` and the library paths of the R session that ran
`use_hooks()`, and runs R without the project's `.Rprofile` or
`.Renviron`. If you upgrade R or move your library, run `use_hooks()`
again; `status()` reports a hook whose `Rscript` has gone.

When the repository already has a `commit-msg` hook from another tool, or
uses a hook manager (`core.hooksPath`), `use_hooks()` leaves it alone,
writes its script to `.git/weft/commit-msg`, and prints the line to add to
the hook you already run.

`git commit --no-verify` skips every hook for one commit. It is there for
emergencies, such as R being broken. It is not a way past a finding:
answer the finding instead. `use_hooks(remove = TRUE)` removes the hook.

## What the reader sees: the rendered-output check

Some mistakes show only after Quarto has done its work. A cross-reference
to a label that does not exist prints "?@sec-missing". A value that was
missing prints "NA". A fence Pandoc did not read prints ":::" in the text.
A third filter, `weft-output.lua`, reads the finished document after
Quarto's own filters, in every output format, and looks for three things:

| Kind | Finds | Setting | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| unresolved reference | under Quarto, "?@sec-missing" for a cross-reference, and "?meta:key" or "?var:key" for a shortcode, where Quarto found nothing | `output_refs` | `fail` |
| missing value in output | `NA`, `NaN`, `Inf` or `-Inf` (also `nan`, `inf`, `-inf`) as a word in prose, headings, lists, footnotes and captions | `output_missing` | `warn` |
| leftover markup | text that starts with `:::`, an attribute block stuck to a word, such as `m{.num}`, and under Quarto bookdown's `\@ref(` | `output_markup` | `fail` |

Each setting is `fail`, `warn` or `off`, in `_weft.yml` or under a
document's `weft:` key. A Quarto project collects the findings with the
other failures and reports them once, after the render, naming each format
in which a finding occurred:

```{verbatim, lang = "text"}
weft: 1 failure
  ch2.qmd #sec-methods (html)  [unresolved reference] ?@sec-missing
      As shown in ?@sec-missing, the flow was low.
    Quarto could not resolve the reference `@sec-missing`, and printed "?@sec-missing" (rule 2.5.5).
weft: 1 warned check(s)
  ch2.qmd #sec-results (html)  [missing value in output] NA
      The mean was NA across the sites.
    "NA" in the rendered prose: a value printed as missing. Mark a deliberate one [NA]{.weft-literal why="..."} (rule 2.5.5).
```

An "NA" that is meant, such as an abbreviation, is marked
`[NA]{.weft-literal why="not applicable"}`. Table cells, code and raw
content are not searched for missing values, so "NA" in a table is never
reported. "N/A", "NULL" and "None" are not matched.

What it cannot check:

- citations: a filter sees a citation before the citation processor runs,
  so an unknown key cannot be told from a known one. The `cite-key` lint
  checks keys against the bibliography;
- what a writer or a later program adds: bookdown's `\@ref()` under R
  Markdown, LaTeX's "??", Typst's own references.

Two filters can name the same text. `bare_missing` warns at knit time
about a bare value that prints `NA`, naming its expression, and the output
check warns about the same "NA" in the output, naming its sentence. The
`weft-check` filter fails on a weft attribute block it could not read,
before Quarto's filters, and the output check may list the same text again
as leftover markup. Neither pair is merged.

The filter must run after Quarto's, which an extension cannot arrange, so
`use_quarto()` adds an entry of its own to `_quarto.yml` (see
`vignette("setup", package = "weft")`). **A project set up before this
check gets it only when you run `use_quarto()` again** (or `use_setup()`
again for an R Markdown document outside Quarto). Until then `status()`
says what is missing:

```text
  quarto       missing   missing: _extensions/weft-check/weft-output.lua; _quarto.yml lacks the weft entries (the weft-output.lua filter entry, `at: post-render`)
```

`verify()` collects the findings in its render part: each `fail` finding
fails it, and `warn` findings are listed. Its result holds them in
`output`.

## Before release: `verify()`

`verify()` is the full check. It has four parts:

| Part | What it does |
|---|---|
| `lints` | runs the tier-1 lints over the whole project and compares them with a commit |
| `decisions` | checks the `decision` pointers in `dict.yml` and in the documents: on `.weft-literal` and `cite` spans, and in `claim()` calls that give a literal `decision` |
| `render` | renders every document with Quarto (or knits it, under R Markdown), backing up and restoring `_freeze`, and reads the record each render leaves to see that every check ran and passed; it also collects the findings of the rendered-output check, below |
| `ledger` | checks that no ledger is stale |

```{r}
weft::verify()
#> weft verify: passed
#>   lints      1 tolerated finding
#>   decisions  0 pointers
#>   render     1 document rendered
#>   ledger     1 ledger checked
#>
#> Tolerated findings (rule 8.1.2); make a rule strict in _weft.yml when its count is 0:
#>   numeral         1 remain
#> weft verify: 4.7 s
```

The tolerated finding is the "2024" committed before weft. The count is a
measure of how far adoption has come. When a rule's count reaches 0, add
it to `strict` in `_weft.yml`, and `verify()` then fails on any instance
at all.

A render re-writes the ledgers. Commit them after `verify()` if they
changed.

When something is wrong, `verify()` says what and fails. Here the Lower
reading was mistyped as 79:

```{r}
weft::verify()
#> weft verify: failed
#>   lints      1 tolerated finding
#>   decisions  0 pointers
#>   render     quarto exited with status 1; 1 failure, 0 not executed
#>   ledger     1 ledger checked
#>
#> Knit-time failures
#>   report.qmd
#>        17  failed claim  . < u(50, NTU) was FALSE (value 79 [NTU])
#>                          `r claim(max(turbidity), . < u(50, NTU))`
#>
#> Tier-2 findings on added lines
#>   report.qmd
#>        17  claim-word  Claim word "highest" in a sentence with a value; check that the value still bears it out, or guard the word with an `if` span (rule 5.5.1).
#>
#> Tolerated findings (rule 8.1.2); make a rule strict in _weft.yml when its count is 0:
#>   numeral         1 remain
#> weft verify: 4.9 s
#> Error: verify() failed: 2 reason(s); the report is above (rule 8.1.1).
```

A failing `verify()` signals an error of class `weft_verify_error`, so
`Rscript -e "weft::verify()"` exits with status 1. Tier-2 findings are
listed for a reader and never fail it.

Arguments narrow it:

- `verify(static = TRUE)` runs the lints and the decision check only, with
  no render. It takes a second, and needs no data.
- `verify(files = "report.qmd")` renders and judges some documents only.
- `verify(since = "v1.0")` compares the lints with another commit.

```{r}
weft::verify(static = TRUE)
#> weft verify: passed
#>   lints      1 tolerated finding
#>   decisions  0 pointers
#>   render     skipped: static = TRUE
#>   ledger     skipped: static = TRUE
#>
#> Tolerated findings (rule 8.1.2); make a rule strict in _weft.yml when its count is 0:
#>   numeral         1 remain
#> weft verify: 0.3 s
```

`verify_skip` in `_weft.yml` names parts to skip every time, for example
`verify_skip: [render]` for a project whose data are not on every machine.
`status()` reports a skipped part as `off`.

## On pull requests: `use_ci()`

`use_ci()` writes `.github/workflows/weft.yml`, a GitHub Actions workflow
that runs `weft::verify(static = TRUE)` on each pull request, compared with
the branch it will merge into. It needs no data and no Quarto, so it runs
for any project. `use_weft()` skips it unless `origin` is on GitHub.

The workflow catches a commit made with `--no-verify`, or on a machine
without the hook.

## Draft mode

While a chapter is half written, a failing claim or an unfinished span can
get in the way. `draft: true` in `_weft.yml` (or the environment variable
`WEFT_DRAFT=1`) makes a render report its failures and finish, with a
marker such as `<<weft: failed claim, line 20>>` in the output in place of
the value. See `vignette("wording", package = "weft")`.

Draft mode does not change the commit gate, which still runs. `verify()`
refuses to run in draft mode, because a draft render fails nothing:

```{r}
weft::verify()
#> Error: verify() does not run in draft mode (rule 8.1.5): draft is on in _weft.yml. A draft render fails nothing, so it can verify nothing.
```

Turn draft mode off before release. `status()` shows it as `off` while it
is on.

## Seeing the set-up: `status()`

`status()` reports what weft has installed, and what is missing or out of
date:

```{r}
weft::status()
#> weft status: creek-report
#>   setup        ok        _weft.yml records weft 0.1.0 (installed: 0.1.0)
#>   activation   ok        route found (the .Rprofile)
#>   quarto       ok        extension, scripts and _quarto.yml entries are in place
#>   dictionary   ok        dict.yml and its schema are in place
#>   hooks        ok        the commit-msg hook is weft 0.1.0, Rscript /usr/local/bin/Rscript
#>   ci           n/a       origin is not on GitHub
#>   agent docs   ok        the AGENTS.md block and the skill are current
#>   draft        ok        draft mode is off
#>   verify_skip  ok        verify() skips nothing
#>   strict       ok        no rule is strict
#> Nothing to install. Run weft::verify() to check the project.
```

It writes nothing and starts no R process.

## A routine

1. Write. Render as often as you like.
2. Before each commit, read `changes()`. Look at every structural change
   and every new condition.
3. Commit the source and the ledger together. Answer the gate if it
   refuses: compute the number, fix the construct, or add the trailer.
4. Before you hand the report on, turn draft mode off and run `verify()`.
